summary: Describes how to prepare internationalized iSCSI names so that typing and comparing them works sensibly for users around the world. Each iSCSI initiator and target has a globally unique name that must be easy to transcribe and compare. It defines a string profile to make that consistent.

eli5.summary: Names can use letters from many languages, and some look the same but are different. This sets rules so two people writing the same name end up with matching names.

subtitle: Rules that turn iSCSI device names into a plain, lower-case, comparable form, whatever language they were typed in.

tldr.problem: iSCSI initiators and targets need globally unique names that people can transcribe by hand and that simple embedded software can compare byte for byte.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a stringprep profile: map characters to lower case or equivalent, normalize with Unicode form KC, and prohibit a long list of characters, including white space and most ASCII punctuation.
tldr.outcome: Names come out in one canonical form, so different implementations compare them the same way. Differences could otherwise give an initiator access to the wrong target.

today: RFC 3722 is a Proposed Standard, published in April 2004. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The iSCSI protocol (RFC 3720) lets hosts reach SCSI devices over an IP network. Its end-points, called initiators and targets, each have a globally unique name defined in RFC 3721.

An iSCSI name is a string of UTF-8 characters with a type designator, a naming authority based on domain names, and a unique part. The unique part may be generated from anything the naming authority likes, and may include user input.

RFC 3722 describes how to prepare such internationalized names so that entering and comparing them makes sense for typical users around the world. It says the profile MUST be used with the iSCSI protocol.
sections.eli5: Every disk and computer in an iSCSI setup has a name, like a name tag. This document says how to write the name tags so everyone reads them the same way.

sections.title: Why Names Need a Profile
sections.content:
Names may be transcribed between administrators by email, voice or paper, so a case-insensitive comparison would be desirable. But initiators and targets must compare names often, mostly in simple embedded software, so case-sensitive comparison is highly desirable for implementors.

A fully case-sensitive scheme would treat example-name and Example-Name as different, which causes confusion when names are transcribed. The goal is names that users can enter and that can be compared byte for byte with minimal confusion.

The answer is to normalize names: a normalized character set converted to lower case or equivalent, no white space, and very limited punctuation.
sections.eli5: People do not care if a name is written in capitals, but simple computers do. So the rule is to always write names in small letters, and then everyone and every machine agrees.

sections.title: Mapping and Normalization
sections.content:
This profile is a profile of stringprep from RFC 3454, which requires a profile to state its character repertoire, mappings, normalization, and prohibited output. The input and output repertoire is Unicode 3.2.

For mapping, the tables B.1 and B.2 from RFC 3454 MUST be used when generating iSCSI names from Unicode characters. For normalization, Unicode normalization form KC MUST be used.

For users of ASCII only, any upper-case characters input through a user interface MUST be mapped to their lower-case equivalents.
sections.eli5: First you swap every capital letter for its small version, and tidy up look-alike ways of writing the same letter, so there is only one way to spell each name.

sections.title: Allowed and Prohibited Characters
sections.content:
For ASCII, the allowed characters are the dash, the dot, the colon, lower-case letters a to z and digits 0 to 9.

The profile prohibits the characters in RFC 3454 tables C.1.1, C.1.2, C.2.1, C.2.2, C.3, C.4, C.5, C.6, C.7, C.8 and C.9. It adds two prohibitions of its own:

  • U+3002 (ideographic full stop), because many domain name input mechanisms, particularly in Asia, use it as if it were the ASCII dot U+002E.
  • Other ASCII characters in the range U+0000 to U+007F, other than the dash, dot and colon. They are reserved for future use in protocol elements such as URIs.

Bidirectional strings are checked as described in RFC 3454 section 6. If the processing in RFC 3720 calls for a list of unassigned code points, table A.1 from RFC 3454 is that list. The iSCSI protocol has further naming rules that are checked outside this profile.
sections.eli5: Only a few simple marks are allowed in a name: a dash, a dot, a colon, small letters and numbers. Spaces and odd symbols are banned so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ISO/IEC 10646 has many characters that look similar, and users may compare names visually, for example when comparing the names of trusted third parties. This profile does nothing to map similar-looking characters together.

An initiator may use a name to check that a discovered target is the correct one, and a target may use it to decide whether an initiator is allowed access. If implementations interpret and compare names differently, an initiator could gain access to the wrong target, or be denied access to a legitimate one.
sections.eli5: Some letters from different alphabets look the same to your eyes. This document does not fix that, but it makes sure all computers at least compare names the same way.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: This is a stringprep profile, and it has been registered in the IANA Stringprep Profiles registry, following the process described in the IANA Considerations section of RFC 3454. The RFC says most of its text was copied from the stringprep profile for Internationalized Domain Names, RFC 3491.
sections.eli5: The rulebook was written down in an official list, so anyone can look it up.

items.title: Prohibited output
items.text: Tables C.1.1 to C.9 plus U+3002 and most ASCII punctuation.
